newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden seeks to calm budget fears.
newsitem.headline: Sweden seeks to calm budget fears.

text.p: The Swedish government launched a damage control exercise on Friday to try to persuade financial markets that it had not surrendered its two-year-old policy of strict fiscal discipline.

Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said the announcement two days ago that 10 billion crowns ($1.4 billion) more in state spending would be allocated to welfare services from next year did not represent a change of policy.
"I am completely convinced that we will still have very strict budgetary discipline in Sweden," Asbrink told reporters.

The Swedish crown has fallen and interest rates risen since Prime Minister Goran Persson earlier this week announced he was planning a 10 billion crown pay-out in 1998. On Thursday he said the 10 billion would be a permanent spending commitment.
Critics have accused the Social Democratic Party prime minister of blatant electioneering as the money is first scheduled to be distributed next year, when a general election will be held.

Asbrink said the Swedish economy was developing more favourably than expected and that the budget deficit would be just over three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1996 compared with an earlier forecast of four percent.

"The development has been more favourable than we had estimated in the autumn. In September we forecast a budget deficit for 1996 of about four percent. Now we see it will be just over three percent," Asbrink said.
Asbrink repeated that the government's budget goals remained.
"This means that there will be a budget deficit below three percent in 1997 and this we will reach with a wide margin.
"In 1998 we will have a balanced budget and the third goal is a budget surplus after 1998, meaning 1999 and thereafter. We have not changed, weakened or postponed this goal," he said.
He said he was not worried about the market reaction in the past few days since the plan was announced. Swedish debt yields have risen and the crown has weakened.
"I am not concerned about the development on particular days. The trend in the Swedish economy is what the market should look at. The development is in an unequivocally positive direction," he said.
Asbrink said the 10 billion crowns could also be put towards cutting some taxes.
"The sectors we will prioritise are employment, as well as health care, care for the elderly, child care, education and environmental issues in order to have a sustainable country," Asbrink said.

"The measures in 1998 will not consist entirely of payments. Part can be used to reduce tax and cutting employer fees is also a possibility. The measures will be foremost aimed at small and medium-sized companies," Asbrink said.
Asbrink said much needed to be done before it was established exactly how the money would be allocated. The final plan would be mapped out in the spring budget due in April.
Analyst James McKay at U.S. investment bank Painewebber said the election process was playing a growing role in Swedish economic policy.
"There is a growing risk that we will see more populist policies, that is to say tax cuts and so on, because of the election," he said.

Handelsbanken Chief Economist Carl Hamilton said the pledge to commit 10 billion crowns might be unwise because it was too early for the government to be sure the money would be there. "Budget forecasts are notoriously difficult. It is not possible today to do a precise budget forecast for 1998," he said. ($1=7.212 Swedish Crown)
